title: Advanced Topics
oneLiner: Where it's all heading: models that see and hear by turning pictures and sound into tokens, read enormous documents, reason and use computers, and the full stack and safety work behind real products.

what.html:
Everything in this course works on tokens. Images become tokens by cutting them into patches; sound becomes tokens by slicing it into short frames or codes. Put them in one sequence and a single model can read, see and listen. Meanwhile context windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to a million, frontier models reason at length and use tools, and real products stitch all the pieces into one stack, with safety testing that grows alongside capability.

Everyday versionA translator who used to read only letters now also looks at photos, listens to voice notes, keeps an entire archive open on the desk, uses a calculator and a browser, and works under a supervisor who checks the riskiest decisions.

why.html:
• Voice and vision assistants are built on these ideas.
  • Understanding costs helps you design realistic products.
  • Capability and safety must grow together.

how.title: Pictures as tokens
how.html: A 224 × 224 image cut into 16 × 16 squares gives 196 patch tokens, which a small adapter maps into the language model's word space.

how.title: Sound as tokens
how.html: 10 seconds of speech becomes 500 short frames, or 6,000 codec tokens that a model can also generate to speak back.

how.title: Huge contexts
how.html: From about 2,000 to a million tokens: memory grows in step, but the comparisons attention makes grow with the square of the length.

how.title: Frontier abilities
how.html: Long thinking, tools inside reasoning, operating computers, and working on multi-hour tasks, limited mainly by reliability and cost.

how.title: Putting it all together
how.html: A real assistant uses a tuned model, document search, an agent loop, filters, efficient serving and tests. One request might use about 7,000 input tokens and cost about 3 cents.

how.title: Bigger isn't automatically safer
how.html: More capable models need more careful testing: dangerous-skill checks, red teams, gradual release and clear documentation.

demo.html: Match each description to the advanced topic.

example.html:
Counting image tokens. 224 ÷ 16 = 14 patches per side; 14 × 14 = 196 tokens. Double the resolution to 448 and you get 28 × 28 = 784 tokens: four times the context for one picture.

Supplementary Small, distilled and quantized models now run on phones and laptops, trading some capability for privacy, speed and cost.

misunderstandings: Multimodal models need a different kind of brain.
They reuse the same Transformer on new tokens.
A million-token window means perfect recall.
Use of long context must be tested.
Frontier models no longer need safeguards.
Each layer adds cost and failure points.
takeaways: Audio → frames (50/s) or codec tokens (K × rate); shared token space.
Context grew ~2k → 1M; KV linear, attention quadratic.
Frontier: long reasoning, tools, computer use, multimodality.
Integrated stack with evaluation; capability and safety scale together.
thirty: Multimodal models reuse Transformers on new token types. Images: ViT patches (224² with 16² patches → 196 tokens), embedded and projected (768 → 4096) into the LLM space, interleaved with text; resolution drives token count. Audio: encoder frames (20 ms → 50/s) or neural-codec tokens (8 codebooks × 75 Hz → 600/s) that also enable speech generation; a shared token space allows any-to-any modelling. Context windows grew from ~2k to ~1M tokens: KV memory grows linearly, attention pairs quadratically (~238,000× from 2k to 1M), enabled by FlashAttention, Ring Attention, RoPE scaling, GQA/MLA and paged caches; effective use must be tested. Frontier systems add RL-trained long reasoning, native tool and computer use, and long-horizon agents; reliability, cost and oversight become the limits. Products integrate model, alignment, prompting, RAG, agents, guardrails, efficient serving and evaluation (≈7,080 input tokens ≈ $0.03 per request in the example). Frontier risks require dangerous-capability evaluations, red teaming, staged deployment and transparency.
